analysis.one_liner: Extends federal anti-discrimination and equal pay protections to independent contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Education and Labor Committee with zero cosponsors until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change six federal laws — including the Civil Rights Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and the Fair Labor Standards Act — so that independent contractors count as "employees" for anti-discrimination purposes. That would mean gig workers, freelancers, and other contractors could sue if they were fired, paid less, or refused work because of their sex, race, age, religion, disability, or genetic information. The bill was never considered by the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent contractors — gig drivers, freelance workers, and others who are paid as businesses rather than employees — would gain the right to sue over discrimination. Federal workplace discrimination law currently covers "employees," so a contractor who is dropped because of her race or age generally has no federal discrimination claim. The bill would also extend the Fair Labor Standards Act's equal-pay requirement for men and women to contractors [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Adds independent contractors to the definition of covered workers under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act (race, sex, religion, national origin), the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Rehabilitation Act, and the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, so contractors could bring the same discrimination claims employees can [S2][S3].
Extends the Fair Labor Standards Act's equal-pay provision — which requires equal pay for men and women doing the same work — to individuals who provide work under an independent contract [S3].
The change is defined broadly: any 'individual who provides work for an employer under the terms of an independent contract with such employer' is covered, no matter the industry [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on independent contractors — gig platforms, staffing arrangements, and businesses of any size that hire contractors — would bear the cost. They would face potential discrimination lawsuits they are currently exempt from, plus the compliance burden of applying anti-discrimination and equal-pay rules to their contractor relationships [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill never attracted a single cosponsor, which is a sign that even allies of workplace-protection legislation saw problems with treating all independent contractors as employees across six statutes at once [S4].

The definition sweeps in every independent contractor, including genuinely self-employed professionals; some businesses and workers argue that reclassifying all contractors as covered employees could make companies more hesitant to hire contractors at all, reducing the flexibility that draws many people to gig and freelance work. The bill text does not include a carve-out for these arrangements [S3].

The Fair Labor Standards Act amendment is narrow — it changes only the equal-pay provision (section 6(d)) rather than the whole statute — so on minimum wage and overtime questions the bill does less than its title suggests [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Extending basic anti-discrimination protections to contractors is a real gain for a large and growing group of workers who currently have almost no federal recourse if they are dropped or underpaid because of who they are. The costs fall on the companies that use contractors, and the objection that a blanket reclassification could chill contractor hiring is a fair one — but the bill got no debate, no amendments, and no cosponsors, so there was never a chance to weigh these trade-offs or narrow the design.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the bill on August 31, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S1][S5].
No cosponsors signed on, no committee action was ever taken, and the bill never reached the House floor [S4][S5].
The bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that classify workers as independent contractors — gig platforms foremost among them — are better off, because the bill died and they continue to be exempt from federal anti-discrimination and equal-pay law for their contractor workforce.

for.name: Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.role: Sponsor; non-voting Delegate representing the District of Columbia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it at introduction; it was her bill alone.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never reported the bill, held no markup, and never sent it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no recorded opposition — the bill had one Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and simply expired in committee [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Gig economy platforms (ride-hailing, delivery, freelance marketplaces)
industries.note: These businesses classify their workers as independent contractors precisely to avoid employee obligations; the bill would have exposed them to discrimination and equal-pay claims for the first time. Because the bill died, their exemption remains intact.

industries.industry: Businesses that rely on contractor labor generally (staffing, consulting, small firms)
industries.note: Any employer using independent contracts would have faced new litigation exposure and compliance costs. Their gain from inaction runs against the interest of the contractors who work for them.
